title: The master craftsman and the Cossack
sentences: Together with my travelling companion we were disguised as Hungarian cowboys.
Our dress was a round, brimmed hat, low-heeled cowhide boots, baggy trousers, a fancy tobacco pouch dangling at the hip, and a pick.
With our dust-covered, sunburnt faces, we would have passed for outlaws anywhere you cared to look.
At Arad, his trembling colleagues urged the representative to shave off his moustache for the sake of greater anonymity.
The poor fellow was terribly frightened; he took up a razor, sat before a mirror, twisted his moustache first to the right, then to the left…
a tear fell from his eye…
then he put the razor down again: "I'd rather lose my neck after all!"
he said, and the moustache remained.
Three fine peasant horses were harnessed to our wagon; we both sat on the driver's seat, the brandy flask and the canvas-walled saddlebag hung from the shaft.
In it were bacon and five-day-old bread.
One morning, on a side road through the Hibari woods, we came upon a remarkable little man.
Clearly he was a fugitive too.
He wore a tall hat with a broad crown; his face was shaved from the nose to the ear,
which left his small face with a disproportionately enormous chin and an even wider mouth in the most marvellous state of exaggeration, and the sleeves of his ill-fitting frock coat,
even though turned up, reached to the tips of his fingernails, while the long swallowtail neatly brushed his ankles.
From the pocket of his grey trousers the handle of an alarmingly large pair of tailor's shears dangled with great ostentation.
— This is the man we need — said I, turning to my companion —,
if we take him onto our wagon, whoever sees us will think he engaged us as drivers.
— Would they not take me aboard, good sir?
— the man shouted to us from afar.
— Gladly, if you wish.
— But where are you gentlemen going?
— We are going everywhere — I answered, and the more I looked at him, the more familiar his features began to seem.
Two years earlier I had seen him on some small-town stage; he was an actor, and a bad one — in Hamlet he was the ghost.
— But where are you going, really?
— he asked me in a plaintive voice.
— Well, let us say to Borsod county.
(I knew well enough: he was a landowner from those parts, who sometimes wandered with actors out of sheer restlessness.)
The man climbed onto the wagon, swearing that he could not pay more than five kreutzers for the fare, for he had been robbed on the road, and other such tales.
that he was a tailor's apprentice from Böszörmény, on his way to Kövesd about some inheritance, and told a border anecdote from the eventful sphere of apprenticeship,
and when he had thoroughly finished his made-up role, turning back to him I asked: "when did you last play Hamlet's father?"
The man's face turned blue-green with fright.
Even the cowboys know him; but when he then recognized me in turn,
his mouth stretched to both ears; he wept and laughed, fell upon my back (for he could not reach me from the front),
and then told how the theatrical company with which he had wandered had en masse deserted Thalia's banner for the Hungarian defenders.
He shared that fate as well.
There he was for a long time the army's chief jester; later:
when the chief surgeon died and the second surgeon was promoted to his place, he was appointed to fill the vacant second-surgeon's post.
— But surely you knew nothing of that trade.
— Some officer recommended me for the office, to whom I had greatly pleased in Nagyvárad, in The Barber of Seville, as Doctor Bartolo.
Besides, there were any number of doctors like myself in the army.
— Did you heal anyone?
— Indeed, matters took a most curious turn for me.
During the battle of Debrecen, while the cannon thundered on, they seated me beside a haystack, so that the wounded might be brought there.
Once a handsome young artilleryman was led toward me by two others, arm in arm; the young man stopped before me,
he raised his two bloody arms: "Look, doctor, I no longer have even one hand," he said sadly.
As he was loading the cannon, a ball carried off both his hands at once.
The world turned away from me; I grew dizzy and threw myself backward into the ditch.
They doused me with cold water in that state.
By then another wounded man was brought there as well; both his legs had been shot off,
and as one leg was carried off by the ball, he begged the comrade standing beside him to push him aside, for they would surely shoot off the other leg next,
and before his comrade could help him, another cannonball struck precisely there and tore off his other leg as well.
I would rather have stood before the cannon than have witnessed such wounds.
I had scarcely bandaged them when the army began to flee; the poor fellows were left behind — they were fortunate if they could die.
when we emerged from the forest, we saw Cossack horsemen galloping toward us from afar.
They spotted us; we could not turn back into the woods.
The most prudent advice in such a situation was to press forward with a good conscience.
A few minutes later they surrounded us and halted our wagon.
A shaggy warrior in a peaked cap on a short stout pony, a three-and-a-half-ell lance in his hand, a long musket slung crosswise on his back,
rode up to me, and before I could rummage through the few Slovak sentences still lodged in my memory, he addressed me — brokenly, but understandably — in Hungarian.
— Where do you come from?
that for the first moment I did not know in what language to answer his question.
(Later I learned that this hetman was a resident of the Croatian borderland, and
as such had long tarried among the Komárom garrison guard, where he learned Hungarian, and then entering the private service of a Russian prince, he later enlisted among the Cossack troops.)
— Where do you come from?
— he shouted at me again, since I had not answered his first question but stood gaping.
— From Ladány — I answered.
— What are you carrying?
— We are driving this gentleman here, who sits in the back.
— What gentleman? — the Cossack snarled at me.
I looked back.
Of my doctor neither trace nor tidings.
No one sat in the wagon bed.
The Cossacks, however, had already begun to poke with their spears in the coal heaped in the wagon box,
at which operation the vanished man rose trembling and squealing from the wagon box, where he had hidden in fright.
His wretched appearance, his steeple-topped hat wreathed with strands of hay and straw, and his terrified expression provoked the Cossacks to frightful guffaws,
which the ex-doctor's notion increased, that he should present himself to the threatening Muscovites as a devout Christian,
he began to cross himself — first with one hand, then with both, which looked very strange indeed.
— Who is the gentleman!
— the shaggy Cossack hetman thundered at him.
The man neither saw nor heard, and though they spoke to him in Hungarian, he understood the question to mean that he should hand over his money,
and trembling greatly he reached into his inner pocket and, drawing out a bundle of blue, green and yellow theatre return tickets and labels peeled from wine bottles, handed them to the Cossack.
The wretched fellow thought that this stranger from distant lands must have seen by now in Hungary all manner of banknotes of every colour, shape and inscription:
so that henceforth he would boldly take any coloured printed paper for genuine currency.
But the Cossack could read Hungarian well, and he threw the papers handed over back at the trembling ex-doctor's head so that each one flew off in a different direction,
and then drawing his sword, with bloodshot eyes and no scant profanity he roared at the terrified man.
— Who are you?
You'll die.
What do you want?
What are you?
Seeing that he would not answer but only embroiled us further in trouble, I turned to the hetman and offered him the flask:
— Leave that poor wretch alone, neighbour.
He is a tailor's apprentice and nothing more.
— Yes, yes!
— my man nodded his head, bobbing hastily and illustrating his claim with comic pantomime, miming sewing with a needle.
The hetman laughed heartily, then took a long pull from my flask, and returning it, stripped off his upper jacket with great nonchalance,
and showing a large tear on his back, tossed it to the doctor, curtly commanding him to mend it.
Amid much fumbling he found needle and thread in his pockets, slipped the thimble onto his finger, snapped and waxed the thread in tailor's fashion,
laid the jacket on his knee and sewed with great greed and haste until he had stitched and cut such a botched patch on the jacket in question that the general himself could wear it.
The Cossacks followed every stitch with curious laughter, and their good humour was terrible,
when the doctor tried to return the mended jacket to the hetman, it turned out that while mending it he had sewn it to his own knee.
The hetman took another pull from my flask, then let us know we might go wherever we pleased,
but he would take the tailor with him, for every garment in his company sorely needed his healing operations, and without waiting for his consent,
he seized the little man by the collar of his frock coat and, lifting him from the wagon, seated him beside himself on the saddle at the rear.
And with that, clattering and jingling, he galloped off with his shaggy companions into the fallen leaves whence they had come.
The little doctor clung on trembling with both hands from either side.
I knew he would come to no harm.
When two weeks later I drifted into Zemplén, he was already long since a schoolmaster in some Palóc village,
from which the cantor had gone off as a guerrilla and hacked the young Scythians to pieces as though the hazel tree had been born in the palm of his hand.
